Let p1​,…,pa​ be the primes not exceeding x​, where a=π(x​), and let Φ(x,a) count integers 1≤n≤x divisible by none of these primes. Every surviving integer other than 1 is prime: a composite integer at most x has a prime factor at most its square root. Conversely, the surviving primes are exactly those between x​ and x. Thus the Legendre prime-counting formula is
π(x)=Φ(x,π(x​))+π(x​)−1(x≥1).​
(1)
By inclusion-exclusion,
Φ(x,a)=∑S⊆{1,…,a}​(−1)∣S∣⌊∏i∈S​pi​x​⌋,
(2)
where the empty product is one. To cover literally every positive real x, replace the subtraction of 1 by 1{x≥1}​: for 0<x<1, both counts are zero and there is no surviving integer 1.
For x=48, the sieving primes are 2,3,5. The surviving count is 48−(24+16+9)+(8+4+3)−1=13. Consequently
π(48)=13+3−1=15.​
(3)

Words: 98
2F OurBigBook.com
The two-dimensional Brouwer fixed-point theorem states that every continuous map from a closed filled triangle to itself has a fixed point. Use the triangle Δ={x∈R3:xi​≥0, ∑i​xi​=1}, which lies in a two-dimensional affine plane. Strict positivity of the matrix entries ensures (Ax)i​>0 for every x∈Δ. Therefore
T(x)=∑i​(Ax)i​Ax​
(4)
is a continuous self-map of Δ, in fact into its interior. Its fixed point x satisfies Ax=λx, where λ=∑i​(Ax)i​>0. Since x=T(x) lies in the interior, A has an eigenvector all of whose entries are strictly positive. This is positive matrix eigenvector from simplex normalization; it uses strict positivity, not merely nonnegative entries.

3G (Geometry of Group Actions)

Words: 186 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 186
3G OurBigBook.com
For a Euclidean circle with centre c and radius r, two distinct finite points are inverse when they lie on the same ray from c and their distances from c have product r2. Points on the circle are fixed, and c and infinity are inverse to each other. In complex coordinates this uniquely defines inversion in a circle by
IΓ​(z)=c+z−cr2​.
(5)
Uniqueness follows from the ray and product conditions, including the specified centre–infinity pair; the formula also gives IΓ2​=id. A circle through infinity is a straight line in the complex plane; its inversion is reflection in that line, fixing infinity. For a line through c with direction angle θ, its formula is c+e2iθz−c​.
Thus every inversion is an anti-Möbius transformation, of the form (az+b)/(cz+d) with nonzero determinant. If J(z)=z, write such an inversion as M∘J with M a Möbius transformation. Since J∘M∘J is the Möbius transformation with conjugated coefficients, the product of two inversions is M1​∘(J∘M2​∘J), hence Möbius. Pairing consecutive inversions proves every composition of an even number of inversions is a Möbius transformation.

4G (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 272 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 272
4G OurBigBook.com
A binary linear-feedback shift register stores L bits, shifts them at each clock step, and inserts a fixed linear combination over F2​ of the stored bits. Its output obeys a recurrence sn​+c1​sn−1​+⋯+cL​sn−L​=0. Write its connection polynomial as C(D)=1+c1​D+⋯+cL​DL; the corresponding monic feedback polynomial is zLC(z−1).
The Berlekamp-Massey algorithm maintains the shortest recurrence fitting the observed prefix. Initialize C=B=1, length L=0, displacement m=1, and previous nonzero discrepancy b=1. At symbol n, calculate d=sn​+∑j=1L​cj​sn−j​. If d=0, increase m. If d=0, save T=C and replace C by C−(d/b)DmB. If 2L≤n, replace L by n+1−L, B by T, b by d, and m by 1; otherwise only increase m. In the binary field subtraction equals addition. The shifted previous discrepancy polynomial cancels the current discrepancy while preserving earlier equations. A failed recurrence of length L at position n requires a corrected length at least n+1−L when this exceeds L, explaining the length update. Thus the algorithm recovers the shortest compatible register; a known bound L and at least 2L output symbols suffice to identify its minimal recurrence.
For the printed twelve-bit prefix, the nonzero discrepancies occur at positions n=0,1,2,5,6,7 (indexing from zero). The successive updated pairs (L,C) are
(1,1+D),(1,1),(2,1+D2),(4,1+D2+D3),(4,1+D+D2),(4,1+D+D4).
(6)
All remaining discrepancies vanish. Therefore
sn​=sn−1​+sn−4​(n≥4),z4+z3+1 is the shortest compatible feedback polynomial.​
(7)
The first four observed bits are the fill. Length four is necessary: a length-three recurrence would need to hold already at n=3 and no such recurrence fits the prefix. Indeed the equations at n=3,4,5 force c2​=1, c1​+c3​=0, c1​+c3​=1, a contradiction. Finite observations cannot rule out longer nonminimal registers.

6B OurBigBook.com
The terms u and αv represent intrinsic exponential population growth. The losses −uv and −αuv describe competition between the species; −ϵ1​u2 and −αϵ2​v2 describe crowding within each species. The positive constant α sets the relative time scale of the second population.
The four equilibrium points in the nonnegative quadrant are
(0,0),(1/ϵ1​,0),(0,1/ϵ2​),(u∗​,v∗​)=(1−ϵ1​ϵ2​1−ϵ2​​,1−ϵ1​ϵ2​1−ϵ1​​).
(12)
The last follows by solving ϵ1​u+v=1 and u+ϵ2​v=1 and is strictly positive under the assumptions. The Jacobian matrix is
J=(1−v−2ϵ1​u−αv​−uα(1−u−2ϵ2​v)​).
(13)
At the origin its eigenvalues are 1,α>0, so it is unstable. At the first single-species equilibrium they are −1 and α(1−1/ϵ1​)<0; at the second they are 1−1/ϵ2​<0 and −α. Both are asymptotically stable. At coexistence,
J∗​=(−ϵ1​u∗​−αv∗​​−u∗​−αϵ2​v∗​​),detJ∗​=αu∗​v∗​(ϵ1​ϵ2​−1)<0.
(14)
Thus coexistence is a saddle; either species-only equilibrium is stable, and extinction is unstable. The saddle's stable manifold separates the competing basins of attraction.

Choose binary expansions x=0.b1​b2​… that do not end in an infinite string of ones. The doubling map deletes the first digit: F(x)=0.b2​b3​…. Given x and any neighbourhood of it, choose N sufficiently large that its binary cylinder of length N is small enough, and choose a point y sharing that prefix but with a prescribed tail. After N shifts, the tail of y may be chosen arbitrarily in [0,1). Choose it close to zero or close to one, whichever is at distance more than 1/3 from FN(x). Then ∣x−y∣≤2−N but ∣FN(x)−FN(y)∣>1/3. Hence the map has sensitive dependence on initial conditions, with a uniform separation constant. At dyadic endpoints the cylinder sharing the chosen terminating expansion still contains points arbitrarily close to the endpoint.

ii

Words: 83 Articles: 1
7E OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 83
ii OurBigBook.com
Every nonempty relatively open interval contains a binary cylinder whose points share a finite prefix. Given nonempty open sets U,V, choose such a cylinder C⊂U of length N. After N binary shifts, FN(C) contains [0,1) with the usual half-open cylinder convention. In particular, some point of C maps into V. Thus F is topologically transitive: FN(U)∩V=∅. Equivalently, concatenate a prefix placing the point in U with a tail placing its Nth iterate in V.

iii

Words: 78 Articles: 1
7E OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 78
iii OurBigBook.com
Given a binary cylinder with finite prefix b1​…bN​, repeat a finite block beginning with that prefix indefinitely. The resulting binary sequence is periodic under the shift and represents a periodic point of an interval map of F in the cylinder. If the given prefix consists entirely of ones, append a zero to the block so that its value is less than one; this still preserves the prefix. Since cylinders can be taken inside any nonempty open interval, periodic points are dense.

A point fixed by F4 satisfies (24−1)x∈Z, so x=j/15 for 0≤j≤14. The points with period dividing two are 0,1/3,2/3, corresponding to j=0,5,10. All other twelve points have least period four. Multiplication by two modulo fifteen groups them into the three cycles
(1/15,2/15,4/15,8/15),(3/15,6/15,12/15,9/15),(7/15,14/15,13/15,11/15).​
(15)
This exhausts the requested four-cycles. The displayed order is the dynamical order, and cyclic changes of the starting point describe the same cycle.

11F OurBigBook.com
Reduce the polynomial modulo p, obtaining a nonzero degree-d polynomial over the field Fp​. If a is a root, polynomial division gives fˉ​(X)=(X−a)h(X). Any different root b is a root of h, because b−a=0 is invertible. Induction on degree therefore proves there are at most d distinct roots modulo p.
Every nonzero residue is a root of Xp−1−1 by Fermat's little theorem. The difference between this monic polynomial and the product over all its p−1 nonzero roots has degree at most p−2, yet has p−1 roots. The root bound forces it to vanish identically over Fp​. Thus all coefficients of the corresponding integer polynomial are divisible by p.
For the requested failure modulo p2, take p=7: 6!+1=721=7⋅103, and 103 is not divisible by seven. Hence the prime-square strengthening fails, even though some special primes do satisfy it.

(p−1)!+1≡0(modp).​

12G (Geometry of Group Actions)

Words: 269 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 269
12G OurBigBook.com
A Kleinian group is a discrete subgroup of PSL2​(C), acting as orientation-preserving hyperbolic isometries of H3 and as Möbius transformations of its boundary sphere. Its limit set consists of the accumulation points on the boundary of an orbit Gx with x∈H3; it is independent of that interior base point and is closed. A nonidentity parabolic transformation is conjugate to z↦z+c, c=0. Its iterates on the upper half-space tend to its unique fixed boundary point, infinity in these coordinates. Consequently every parabolic fixed point belongs to the limit set.
The displayed matrix has determinant one, trace two, and is not the identity because a=0. Its fixed-point equation is a(z−w)2=0, so it has exactly the double fixed point w. It is therefore parabolic, and its fixed point is w.
The determinant-one Gaussian-integer matrices form a subgroup of SL2​(C). They are discrete because their entries lie in a discrete lattice: a matrix sufficiently near the identity has every entry equal to the corresponding identity entry. Passing through the quotient by {±I} preserves discreteness, so their Möbius transformations form a Kleinian group.
For w=n/r, n=p+iq and r=0, set a=r2. This gives the Gaussian-integer parabolic construction
T ↔ (1+rnr2​−n21−rn​).​
(28)
All entries lie in Z[i], the determinant is one, and its parabolic fixed point is n/r=w. The points with nonzero p,q,r are dense in the finite complex plane, and their closure on the sphere includes infinity. Since the limit set is closed and contains all these parabolic fixed points, the limit set is the whole Riemann sphere.

The canonical link function is g(μ)=θ=−1/μ. Some conventions reverse the sign and call 1/μ the reciprocal link; this only reverses the regression coefficients. We retain the genuine natural parameter θ=−1/μ.
In the Gamma regression with canonical link, ηi​=xiT​β<0 and μi​=−1/ηi​. Differentiating the independent-observation log-likelihood gives
U(β)=ϕ−1XT(y−μ),I(β)=ϕ−1XTdiag(μi2​)X.​

with the means and information recalculated at each iteration; damping can preserve Xβ<0 and increase the likelihood. Full column rank makes the information positive definite for positive means.

The fixed-point equation is x[ax2+bx+μ−1]=0. Thus
x=0,x±​=2a−b±b2+4a(1−μ)​​​
(35)
when the discriminant is nonnegative. At zero the multiplier is F′(0)=μ, so it is linearly stable for −1<μ<1 and unstable for ∣μ∣>1. At a nonzero fixed point, eliminate μ to obtain the branch and its multiplier:
μ=1−bx−ax2,M=1+bx+2ax2.
(36)
The branch is stable precisely when −2<x(b+2ax)<0. These formulas specify stability throughout the diagram, including any extra flip points outside the region requested.
If b=0 and a>0, the two nonzero branches x=±(1−μ)/a​ exist for μ<1 and have multiplier 3−2μ>1. Thus μ=1 is a subcritical pitchfork bifurcation. If b=0, the branch through zero has x∼(1−μ)/b and M∼2−μ; its stability exchanges with zero at μ=1, a transcritical bifurcation. The two nonzero roots meet at
μsn​=1+b2/(4a),xsn​=−b/(2a),
(37)
where M=1. The graph of μ(x) has nonzero second derivative −2a, proving a saddle-node bifurcation. At zero and μ=−1, the multiplier is −1, indicating a period-doubling bifurcation; generically its nondegeneracy coefficient is a+b2. If a+b2=0, necessarily b=0 here, composition at μ=−1 instead gives F2(x)−x=4b4x5+O(x6). For δ=μ+1>0 small, the leading return equation is −2δx+4b4x5=0, producing a two-cycle with leading amplitudes x∼±[δ/(2b4)]1/4. Its return multiplier is 1+8δ+o(δ)>1. Thus this special case still has a flip bifurcation, but it is degenerate and subcritical rather than the generic cubic normal form.
For a,b>0, the fold lies above μ=1. Between it and the transcritical point, the branch −b/(2a)<x<0 is stable provided its multiplier remains above −1, while the other branch is unstable. For a,b<0, the fold lies below μ=1: immediately above it the branch x<−b/(2a) is stable and the branch between −b/(2a) and zero is unstable; the branch crossing zero becomes stable for μ>1. All these statements are subject to the displayed exact multiplier criterion if the diagram is extended. The sketch uses representative parameter values and stops before additional flips, as stipulated.

A binary relation R on a set is a well-founded relation if every nonempty subset has an R-minimal member, that is, a member with no predecessor inside that subset. Here write xRy when x∈f(y).
Suppose R is well-founded and fix any g:P(b)→b. Call a partial function h:D→b consistent if D is downward closed under R and h(y)=g({h(x):x∈f(y)}) for y∈D. Two consistent partial functions agree on their common domain: otherwise the set of points where they disagree has a minimal member, all of whose predecessors are in both domains and agree, so applying g gives agreement at that member as well, a contradiction. Thus the union of all consistent partial functions is itself a function h:D→b, on a downward-closed domain, and remains consistent. This union is a set, because every such graph is a subset of a×b.
If D=a, choose a minimal member y of a∖D. All predecessors of y lie in D, so extend h to y by the prescribed value g({h(x):x∈f(y)}). The enlarged domain remains downward closed and consistent, contradicting the union's maximality. Hence D=a. The same minimal-disagreement argument proves uniqueness. This establishes the required recursion directly, without invoking an unproved well-founded recursion theorem.
Conversely, if R is not well-founded, choose a nonempty S⊂a such that each y∈S has a predecessor in S. Let T be all points reachable from S by a finite chain of upward R steps, including S. Then
y∈T⟺f(y)∩T=∅.
(45)
For a point reached by a nonempty chain, its preceding point is in T; for a point of S, use its predecessor in S. The converse follows by appending the final step to a chain. Choose b={0,1} and g(B)=1 if 1∈B, zero otherwise. Both h0​≡0 and h1​=1T​ satisfy the required recursion, and they differ because S=∅. This contradicts recursiveness. Therefore f is recursive exactly when its predecessor relation is well-founded, the characterization of a recursive powerset mapping.

We consider finite-dimensional continuous complex representations of SU(2). Its maximal torus is diag(eiθ,e−iθ). The irreducible representations are
Vn​=Symn(C2),n=0,1,2,…,dimVn​=n+1.​

They may be realized as homogeneous polynomials of degree n in two variables, with the induced linear substitution action. Their torus weights are n,n−2,…,−n, each once. The centre −I acts by (−1)n, so precisely the even-n representations descend to SO(3). In physics n=2j labels integral or half-integral spin j.
Here is a classification argument. Average any positive definite Hermitian form over the compact group using normalized Haar measure. The averaged form is invariant, so the orthogonal complement of an invariant subspace is invariant. Repeatedly splitting gives complete reducibility. Differentiate an irreducible representation and complexify to the Lie algebra sl2​, with generators H,E,F satisfying [H,E]=2E, [H,F]=−2F, and [E,F]=H. Torus periodicity gives integer H-weights. Choose a vector v of maximal weight n; then Ev=0. Induction on k using the commutators gives
EFkv=k(n−k+1)Fk−1v.
(56)
The chain terminates: if Fpv=0 and Fp+1v=0, the displayed formula forces n=p≥0. The vectors v,Fv,…,Fnv have distinct weights, span an invariant subrepresentation, and hence span the irreducible representation. Their generator action agrees with SymnC2. Invariance under the Lie algebra is equivalent to invariance under the connected group, completing the classification. Conversely, a nonzero invariant subspace of a symmetric power contains a weight vector by projection onto torus weights. Raising it to the highest weight and then lowering generates every monomial, proving that the symmetric power is irreducible.
The character on the torus is

with the endpoints interpreted by continuity. Every representation has a unique decomposition V≅⨁n≥0​mn​Vn​. Its multiplicities can be computed from character inner products,

In particular, multiplying weight characters yields the Clebsch-Gordan decomposition Vm​⊗Vn​≅Vm+n​⊕Vm+n−2​⊕⋯⊕V∣m−n∣​. Arbitrary unitary Hilbert-space representations of this compact group similarly decompose into Hilbert direct sums of these finite-dimensional irreducibles; the finite-dimensional statement above is the standard representation-theory setting.

Take an open neighbourhood U on which p is one-to-one and a homeomorphism onto its image. By invariance of domain for topological surfaces, that image is open. Shrink U so the image lies in a complex chart (V,z) of R, and use z∘p as a chart of R. These charts cover R. On any overlap their transition is the transition between the original charts of R, restricted to an open set, so is holomorphic with holomorphic inverse. They define the desired complex structure, and in these charts p is locally the identity. Thus p is holomorphic. The openness supplied by invariance of domain is important when the hypothesis is phrased only as a homeomorphism onto the image.
Let f:C→Y be holomorphic and let π:D→Y be the stated covering. Choose a lift of f(0). The covering-space lifting theorem says that a map from a simply connected, locally path-connected domain has a unique lift after fixing this initial point: lift paths from zero, and homotopy lifting makes their endpoint independent of path. Since C is simply connected, this constructs f​:C→D with π∘f​=f. On a small neighbourhood, the lift is a biholomorphic local inverse of π composed with f, so it is holomorphic. Its modulus is less than one, and Liouville theorem therefore makes it constant. Hence every holomorphic map C→Y is constant.

(80)
Orthogonality to the new innovation requires (1−H)P−H=0, hence H=P/(P+1). Since the variables are jointly Gaussian, this orthogonality is independence. Stationary variance gives P=(1−H)2P+1+H2=P/(P+1)+1, so
P2−P−1=0,P=(1+5​)/2,H=(5​−1)/2.​
(81)
The added process noise reflects the fact that the new observation concerns Xn​, not Xn+1​.
For the control calculation choose a quadratic value coefficient R>0. Conditional minimization of x2+u2+RE[(x+u+ε)2] gives K=R/(1+R) and the Riccati equation R=1+R−R2/(1+R), hence R2=R+1. Separation replaces x by its conditional estimate, giving
K=R/(1+R)=H=(5​−1)/2.​
(82)
To determine the average cost without solving an additional state covariance, complete the square:
x2+u2+RE[Xn+12​−x2∣x,u]=R+(1+R)(u+Kx)2.
(83)
With u=−KXn​, the final square is K2Δn2​. In equilibrium the expected telescoping value term is zero, so the minimal cost is
Jˉ=R+(1+R)K2P=1+5​.​
(84)
The identity also proves optimality: conditional mean minimization of the square uniquely selects the stated control. Here 1−K∈(0,1) ensures stable closed-loop estimates, making the equilibrium averaging valid. This is the Scalar delayed-observation LQG regulator.

The left expression has equal cosine and sine coefficients in the variable Sa​; the right expression has those coefficients proportional to cos(J−π/4) and sin(J−π/4). The Pauli matrices obey (n⋅σ)2=I. Expanding the exponential into even and odd powers gives the time-evolution operator
U(t)=e−iHt/ℏ=Icos(γBt/2)+in⋅σsin(γBt/2).​
(93)
For orthogonal states the identity contribution vanishes, so the transition probability is ∣⟨χ′∣n⋅σ∣χ⟩∣2sin2(γBt/2). For spin up to spin down in a static field (Bx​,0,Bz​), only σx​ has the required matrix element. Hence
P↑→↓​(t)=Bx2​+Bz2​Bx2​​sin2(2γBx2​+Bz2​​t​).​
(94)
For the weak rotating transverse field, take H0​=−ℏγBz​σz​/2. The unperturbed energies give E↓​−E↑​=ℏγBz​. The perturbation matrix element is ⟨↓∣V(t)∣↑⟩=−ℏγAeiαt/2. Thus first-order perturbation theory gives
a↓​(t)=2iγA​∫0t​ei(γBz​+α)sds=2ΩγA​(eiΩt−1),Ω=γBz​+α.
(95)
Squaring its magnitude yields
P↑→↓​≈(γBz​+αγA​)2sin2(2(γBz​+α)t​).​
(96)
The hypothesis is ∣γA∣≪∣Ω∣, excluding resonance. At α=0 this is the leading weak-A expansion of the exact static-field formula with Bx​=A. For extremely long times, a small higher-order frequency correction can accumulate phase, so first-order perturbation is not a uniform approximation on arbitrarily long time scales.

Label the two displacements in cell n by un​,vn​, with cell length 2a. Choose the K spring within a cell and the G spring between cells. The equations are
mu¨n​=−(K+G)un​+Kvn​+Gvn−1​,mv¨n​=−(K+G)vn​+Kun​+Gun+1​.
(97)
A Bloch wave (un​,vn​)=(u,v)ei(2aqn−ωt) gives a two-by-two eigenvalue problem, whose determinant is
(K+G−mω2)2−(K+Ge−2iaq)(K+Ge2iaq)=0.
(98)
Thus the alternating-spring chain dispersion relation is
ω±2​(q)=mK+G±K2+G2+2KGcos(2aq)​​.​
(99)
Periodic boundaries require e2iaqN=1, so q=πj/(Na) modulo π/a. There are N distinct wavenumbers in the Brillouin zone −π/(2a)≤q<π/(2a) and two branches, accounting for 2N modes. The minus branch is acoustic, with zero frequency and in-phase motion at the centre; the plus branch is optical, with opposite cell displacements.
Expanding the square root near zero gives
ω−​(q)∼am(K+G)2KG​​∣q∣,ω+​(q)∼m2(K+G)​​[1−2(K+G)2KGa2q2​].​
(100)
At the zone boundary the square root is K−G, so the acoustic maximum is 2G/m​ and the optical minimum is 2K/m​. The frequency gap is therefore
Δω=2K/m​−2G/m​.​
(101)
Quantizing each harmonic mode gives phonons, bosonic excitations of energy ℏω±​(q) and crystal momentum ℏq defined modulo a reciprocal lattice vector. Their group velocity is dω/dq; acoustic phonons carry long-wavelength sound, while optical phonons have a nonzero centre frequency. There is one longitudinal polarization per branch here, and phonon number is not conserved in thermal equilibrium.

A fixed-axis diatomic molecule has one bond-stretch vibrational coordinate q, reduced mass mr​, and angular frequency ω. In the classical harmonic approximation its internal Hamiltonian is p2/(2mr​)+mr​ω2q2/2. The phase-space contribution per molecule is
zvib​=h1​∫R2​exp[−kTp2/(2mr​)+mr​ω2q2/2​]dpdq=hω2πkT​=ℏωkT​.​
(102)
The Gaussian integrals cancel the reduced mass. Extending the small bond displacement to the whole real line is the usual harmonic approximation. There is no rotational factor because the molecular orientation is fixed.
For N identical dilute molecules of total mass M in volume V, translation supplies V(2πMkT/h2)3/2. Including indistinguishability gives
Z=N!1​[V(h22πMkT​)3/2ℏωkT​]N.
(103)
Using Stirling's approximation and defining Q=(V/N)(2πMkT/h2)3/2kT/(ℏω),
F=−NkT(logQ+1),S=−FT​=Nk(logQ+7/2).​
(104)
The 7/2 is 1+5/2: the logarithm contains T5/2, combining three translational quadratic degrees with two vibrational ones. This is a classical result, valid when vibration is thermally classical rather than quantum frozen.

Replace φ by φ+ϵη, with η vanishing on the boundary, and differentiate the action at zero. Integrate the derivative of η by parts:
δS=∫[∂φ∂L​η+∂φ,a​∂L​∂a​η]d4x=∫[∂φ∂L​−∂a​∂φ,a​∂L​]ηd4x.
(105)
The coefficient of η is the functional derivative δS/δφ.
For the electromagnetic action, δFab​=∂a​δAb​−∂b​δAa​. Antisymmetry combines these terms and integration by parts gives
δS=∫[μ0−1​∂a​Fab−Jb]δAb​d4x.
(106)
Thus the inhomogeneous Maxwell equations are ∂a​Fab=μ0​Jb. The definition of F also gives the homogeneous equations ∂[a​Fbc]​=0, equivalently ∂a​Fab=0. These are the two four-vector Maxwell systems.
Unrestricted variation of the alternative component-gradient action instead gives □Ab=μ0​Jb. This is equivalent to the first Maxwell system only when supplemented by the Lorenz gauge ∂a​Aa=0, because
∂a​Fab=□Ab−∂b(∂a​Aa).
(107)
The alternative action is not by itself gauge-invariant; the additional condition must be supplied consistently, not silently omitted.
Expand the tensor square: FabFab​=2[∂bAa∂b​Aa​−∂bAa∂a​Ab​]. Hence
S−S=2μ0​1​∫∂bAa∂a​Ab​d4x.
(108)
Integrating this cross term by parts twice expresses its integral as a boundary term plus ∫(∂a​Aa)2d4x. Under Lorenz gauge it is therefore purely a boundary term. With fixed or vanishing boundary contributions, the two actions have the same variational equations once the additional gauge condition is included. This is the Lorenz-gauge reduction of the electromagnetic action.

Vary the curve by δxc, fixing endpoints. Integration by parts in the kinetic functional gives its Euler-Lagrange equations
dλd​(2gcb​x˙b)−∂c​gab​x˙ax˙b=0.
(109)
Multiplying by gcd/2 and symmetrizing the velocity product gives
x¨d+Γabd​x˙ax˙b=0,Γabd​=21​gdc(∂a​gbc​+∂b​gac​−∂c​gab​).​
(110)
There is no term proportional to x˙ from parameter reparametrization, so this is the affine geodesic equation.
In units c=1, the static spherical vacuum metric is Schwarzschild with f(r)=1−2GM/r. For example, starting from −e2Φdt2+e2Λdr2+r2dΩ2, the vacuum radial equations give [r(1−e−2Λ)]′=0 and Φ′+Λ′=0. Asymptotic flatness and the Newtonian mass fix e2Φ=e−2Λ=1−2GM/r, giving the displayed metric. Time and azimuthal coordinates are cyclic in its geodesic Lagrangian, so
ft˙=E,r2ϕ˙​=h.​
(111)
Normalize the velocity norm to −k, with k=1 for proper-time parametrized massive motion and k=0 for null motion. In the equatorial plane this gives r˙2+f(k+h2/r2)=E2. For a nonradial orbit, h=0 and u=1/r imply r˙=−hdu/dϕ. Therefore
(u′)2+fu2=−h2k​f+h2E2​.​
(112)
Differentiating with f=1−2GMu yields
u′′+u=h2kGM​+3GMu2.​
(113)
It extends across isolated turning points by continuity. The original PDF's later f=1−GMu is inconsistent with this claimed equation: that choice gives u′′+u=kGM/(2h2)+(3GM/2)u2. The intended Schwarzschild factor is 1−2GMu, which we retain.
For massive motion put ℓ=h2/(GM). The Newtonian solution is u0​=(1+ecosϕ)/ℓ. The resonant cosine forcing in 3GMu02​ is 6GMecosϕ/ℓ2, producing the secular correction 3GMeϕsinϕ/ℓ2. Resumming it into a shifted phase gives the precessing-ellipse approximation
u≈ℓ−1[1+ecos(αϕ)],α=1−3GM/ℓ.​
(114)
For finite eccentricity there are also bounded corrections of this same small order: one particular correction is 3GM(1+e2/2)/ℓ2−GMe2cos(2ϕ)/(2ℓ2), besides adjustable homogeneous terms. Thus the simple displayed ellipse captures the secular precession rather than the complete first-order shape correction. Consecutive periapses are separated by 2π/α, so the Schwarzschild perihelion precession per radial orbit is approximately 6πGM/ℓ, forward in the direction of motion.

uR​=2(RA​+R3B​)cosθ,uθ​=−(RA​−R3B​)sinθ.

Substitution gives
uR​=U(2R3a​−2R3a3​)cosθ,uθ​=−U(4R3a​+4R3a3​)sinθ,uϕ​=0.​
(118)
Rotational symmetry about the translation axis forbids a transverse force. Linearity of the Stokes equations and boundary conditions makes the force linear in U; dissipation makes the force on the translating sphere oppose its motion. Thus the drag is axial and proportional to U, without computing the stress integral. Dimensional analysis further gives scale μaU; the exact single-sphere coefficient is 6π.

For side-by-side spheres, reflection in the vertical mid-plane exchanges the spheres while preserving their common velocity, so their axial drags are equal. For vertically aligned spheres, reflection in the horizontal mid-plane exchanges them and reverses velocity; applying linearity to reverse all velocities back restores the original problem and again gives equal axial drag. These are symmetries of the exact two-sphere Stokes problem.
At a distant side-by-side centre, the leading flow produced by one sphere is 3aU/(4b) in the direction of translation. On its axis it is 3aU/(2b). This ambient entrainment lowers the relative velocity of the other sphere. Using Stokes drag law with that relative velocity gives the mutual drag reduction of two distant translating spheres:
Dside​=6πμaU[1−4b3a​+O((a/b)2)],​
(119)
Daxial​=6πμaU[1−2b3a​+O((a/b)2)].​
(120)
The feedback of the corrected force into the other sphere's flow enters at the next order. If the coefficient 6π is needed directly from the preceding solution, its pressure anomaly is p=3μUacosθ/(2R2). At the surface the traction components are tR​=−3μUcosθ/(2a) and tθ​=3μUsinθ/(2a); their axial projection is the constant −3μU/(2a). Integrating over 4πa2 gives the single-sphere force −6πμaUez​, as used above.

For a plane acoustic wave propagating along k, the linear momentum equation and dispersion ω=c0​k give p​=ρ0​c0​u∥​ and u=u∥​k. Therefore the instantaneous acoustic intensity is
p​u=ρ0​c0​∣u∣2k.​
(121)
For harmonic complex amplitudes the time average instead has the factor one half, ⟨I⟩=21​ρ0​c0​∣u∣2k.
For a radial velocity potential, set v=rϕ. The spherical wave equation reduces to vtt​=c02​vrr​, so
ϕ(r,t)=rF(t−r/c0​)+G(t+r/c0​)​.​
(122)
No incoming radiation from infinity means G=0. Linearizing the moving-surface condition at r=a gives ϕr​(a,t)=iωaϵeiωt, with real parts understood. Write the outgoing solution as ϕ=Aeiω(t−(r−a)/c0​)/r. Its radial derivative at a is −A(1+iωa/c0​)eiωt/a2. Therefore the outgoing acoustic field of a pulsating sphere is
ϕ(r,t)=Re{−1+iωa/c0​iωa3ϵ​reiω(t−(r−a)/c0​)​}.​

In the far field the velocity amplitude has magnitude (ω/c0​)∣A∣/r. Multiply its average plane-wave intensity by the spherical area to obtain the mean acoustic power of a pulsating sphere:
⟨P⟩=c0​2πρ0​ω2​∣A∣2=c0​[1+(ωa/c0​)2]2πρ0​ϵ2a6ω4​.​
(124)
This is positive outward radiated power, evaluated to leading quadratic order in the small real displacement amplitude.

The two independent columns of V remain independent after multiplication by invertible S. Since R=SV has zeros below the second row, its leading two-by-two triangular block is invertible. Hence the image under S of the invariant subspace is exactly span(e1​,e2​). This coordinate plane is invariant under A=SAS−1, forcing the bottom-left block to vanish:
A=(B0​CD​).
